title: Checkpoint: Saving and Investing
objective: After this level you can compare saving, stocks, bonds and funds by risk and return.
summary: Every home for money differs in safety, growth and access. From 1928 to 2025, bills, bonds and stocks formed a ladder: higher returns, bigger bumps. Liquid assets turn into cash quickly.

cards.headline: Savings, bonds, stocks, funds: how do you compare homes for money?
cards.body: The US Securities and Exchange Commission boils it down to three questions. How safe will the money be? How fast can it grow? And how readily can you get it back? Chapter 4 has given you the answers.

items.label: Bonds
points: A loan: interest, then face value back

cards.headline: Same $100, three paths
cards.body: From 1928 to 2025, before inflation, $100 grew to about $2,600 in Treasury bills, about $7,750 in 10-year US government bonds and over $1 million in US stocks. Up the ladder, the returns rose and so did the bumps. Funds don't add a new rung: an index fund holds a rung's whole basket and carries the same risks as its index.

cards.headline: The third question: liquidity
cards.body: A liquid asset is one you can turn into cash quickly. A savings account is about as liquid as it gets. Shares on an exchange can nearly always be sold, though perhaps at a bad price. A non-traded REIT generally can't be sold readily at all. That's Level 31's lesson from a new angle: emergency money has to be safe and reachable.

mascot.line: Safe, growing, reachable. You now know which two each home for money is good at.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: Compare by safety, growth and access
Bills, bonds, stocks: higher return, bigger bumps
Stocks are ownership; bonds are loans
Liquid assets turn into cash quickly

questions.prompt: What does it mean to call an asset 'liquid'?

options.label: It can be turned into cash quickly
It pays interest every month
options.rationale: That's about income, not how fast it becomes cash.

options.label: Its price never changes
options.rationale: Liquid assets can still change in price.

options.label: It is backed by the government
options.rationale: Liquidity is about how quickly you can cash out.

questions.explanation: A liquid asset can be readily converted into cash within a short time.

questions.prompt: Which statement fits the 1928 to 2025 ladder of bills, bonds and stocks?

options.label: The safest path also grew the most
options.rationale: Bills were safest and grew the least.

options.label: All three paths grew by about the same amount
options.rationale: Bills reached about $2,600; stocks passed $1 million.

options.label: Higher-returning paths came with bigger bumps
Stocks rose every single year
options.rationale: Stocks lost money in 26 of the 98 years.

questions.explanation: Returns rose up the ladder from bills to bonds to stocks, and so did the losing years.

questions.prompt: From Levels 33 and 34: which pair is right?

options.label: Stock: a loan. Bond: ownership.
Stock: a deposit. Bond: a dividend.
options.rationale: Neither matches: stocks are ownership, bonds are loans.

options.label: Both are loans to a company
options.rationale: Only bonds are loans; stocks are ownership.

options.label: Stock: part-owner. Bond: lender.

questions.explanation: A shareholder owns a slice of the company; a bondholder has lent it money.

questions.prompt: From Levels 36 and 37: an S&P 500 index fund fell sharply in a market crash. Why?

options.label: It carries the same risks as the index it tracks
Index funds hold only one company
options.rationale: They hold the whole basket, or a sample of it.

options.label: Its managers sold everything at the bottom
options.rationale: Index funds are passive and trade rarely.

options.label: Funds are not allowed to diversify
options.rationale: Funds are one of the easiest ways to diversify.

questions.explanation: Diversification protects against single failures, not market-wide falls; an index fund moves with its index.

questions.prompt: Emergency money must be reachable fast. Which of these is the least liquid?

options.label: Cash in a savings account
options.rationale: Savings accounts are about as liquid as it gets.

options.label: Shares traded on an exchange
options.rationale: Exchange-traded shares can nearly always be sold.

options.label: Shares in a non-traded REIT
Notes in your wallet

questions.explanation: Non-traded REITs generally cannot be sold readily, which makes them a poor home for emergency money.
